Name: Direct Prompt Injection Bypasses System Instructions in Customer Support Chatbot
Synopsis: A crafted user message performs a prompt injection that overrides the assistant's system prompt, causing it to ignore its original support-only instructions and follow attacker-supplied commands instead.
Solution: Isolate the system prompt from user-controllable context where the model API supports it, and require a human or policy gate before any consequential action a compromised conversation could trigger.

Name: Indirect Prompt Injection via Poisoned Retrieved Document in RAG Pipeline
Synopsis: A malicious instruction embedded in a third-party document ingested by the retrieval-augmented pipeline performs prompt injection when the model later summarizes that content, causing it to execute attacker-supplied instructions instead of the user's original request.
Solution: Treat retrieved content as untrusted input and strip/flag instruction-shaped text before it reaches the model context; never let retrieved content alone trigger a privileged action.

Name: Jailbreaking Technique Bypasses Content Safety Guardrails on Voice Assistant
Synopsis: A known jailbreaking technique (fictional role-play framing) was used to bypass the voice assistant's content-safety guardrails, a form of prompt injection against its system-level restrictions.
Solution: Apply output-side content filtering as a defense-in-depth layer independent of the system prompt, so a successful jailbreak of the prompt alone isn't sufficient to bypass safety controls.

Name: Prompt Injection via Base64-Encoded Instructions in Support Ticket Field
Synopsis: A support ticket's free-text field contained base64-encoded text that performs prompt injection once decoded and processed by the AI triage agent, bypassing its plain-text input filtering.
Solution: Decode and re-inspect any encoded content before it reaches the model, and never trust that input filtering alone at the raw-text layer will catch an encoded payload.

Name: Multi-Turn Jailbreaking Gradually Erodes System Prompt Adherence
Synopsis: A multi-turn jailbreaking conversation gradually convinced the model to abandon its original system prompt through incremental prompt injection across several turns.
Solution: Re-assert or re-check system-prompt adherence periodically across a long conversation rather than trusting it holds for the entire session.

Name: Prompt Injection in Email Auto-Responder via Forwarded Message Content
Synopsis: The email auto-responder AI processes forwarded message bodies without isolating them from its own instructions, allowing prompt injection through a crafted forwarded email.
Solution: Isolate forwarded/quoted email content from the model's own instructions the same way any other untrusted external input should be isolated.

Name: Jailbreaking via Fictional Framing Bypasses Content Moderation Model
Synopsis: A fictional-narrative framing jailbreaking prompt was used to have the content moderation model approve otherwise-disallowed content, a prompt injection against its safety instructions.
Solution: Combine prompt-level instructions with an independent output classifier so moderation doesn't rely solely on the model's own framing-resistant judgment.

Name: Prompt Injection Through Malicious Code Comments Reviewed by AI Copilot
Synopsis: A code comment containing hidden instructions performs prompt injection when the code-review copilot processes the file, causing it to approve a vulnerable pull request instead of flagging it.
Solution: Never let an AI code-review verdict alone gate a merge - require a human reviewer, and treat code comments as untrusted input the same as any other file content.

Name: Indirect Prompt Injection via Webpage Content Summarized by Browsing Agent
Synopsis: A webpage crawled by the browsing agent contains hidden text that performs prompt injection, redirecting the agent's next actions away from the user's original request.
Solution: Sanitize/strip instruction-shaped text from fetched web content before it enters the agent's context, and require confirmation before the agent takes any action based on browsed content.

Name: Jailbreaking Attempt Using Nested Instruction Override in System Prompt Field
Synopsis: A nested instruction-override payload in a user-supplied field constitutes prompt injection, successfully jailbreaking the assistant into ignoring its configured restrictions.
Solution: Validate and constrain user-supplied fields that flow into the model context, and never let user input directly redefine the assistant's own instruction hierarchy.

Name: System Prompt Leak Exposes Internal Business Rules in AI Support Agent
Synopsis: A crafted user query caused the system prompt to leak in the model's response, exposing internal business rules and escalation criteria that were meant to stay confidential.
Solution: Keep the system prompt free of anything damaging if echoed back, and apply output filtering to catch and block verbatim system-prompt reproduction.

Name: System Prompt Leaked via Repeated-Word Extraction Attack on Chatbot
Synopsis: A known repeated-word extraction technique caused the chatbot's system prompt to leak verbatim into the conversation, revealing internal configuration details.
Solution: Apply output-side detection for verbatim system-prompt reproduction, independent of any single known extraction technique.

Name: Retrieval Pipeline Leaks PII from Training Context to Unauthorized User
Synopsis: The RAG pipeline's system prompt combined with retrieved context caused sensitive customer PII to leak to a user who should not have had access to that record.
Solution: Apply least-privilege data access to the retrieval pipeline so it can never surface a record the requesting user isn't authorized to see, regardless of prompt phrasing.

Name: System Prompt and API Key Reference Leak Through Debug Output
Synopsis: A debug-mode response caused the assistant's system prompt to leak, including a reference to an internal API key placeholder that should never be echoed back to a user.
Solution: Disable verbose/debug response modes in production, and never place a real or placeholder secret reference anywhere the system prompt could echo it.

Name: Model Memorization Causes Leak of Verbatim Training Data Snippet
Synopsis: The deployed model's system prompt instructs it to avoid this, but a targeted query still caused a memorized training data snippet to leak in its output.
Solution: Sanitize/anonymize training data before use so a memorization leak can't expose anything sensitive, since prompt-level instructions alone can't fully prevent memorization leakage.

Name: System Prompt Leak via Translation-Request Side Channel
Synopsis: Asking the assistant to 'translate its instructions' caused its system prompt to leak in translated form, bypassing the direct-request filter that blocks the English-language ask.
Solution: Apply output filtering across all response languages/transformations, not just the direct, untranslated request form.

Name: Cross-Tenant Data Leak from Shared Retrieval Index in Multi-Tenant AI Agent
Synopsis: The system prompt did not scope retrieval to the current tenant, so a query caused another tenant's confidential document to leak into the response.
Solution: Enforce tenant-scoped access control at the retrieval-index layer itself, not just via the system prompt's own instructions.

Name: System Prompt Leak Reveals Proprietary Scoring Logic in Fraud Detection Model
Synopsis: A probing query caused the fraud detection model's system prompt to leak, disclosing proprietary scoring thresholds that inform its risk decisions.
Solution: Keep scoring thresholds and business logic out of the system prompt entirely where possible, storing them server-side and never exposing them to the model's own echoable context.

Name: Summarization Model Leaks Redacted Section of Source Document
Synopsis: Despite the system prompt instructing it to respect redactions, the summarizer's output caused a redacted section of the source document to leak.
Solution: Remove redacted content before it ever reaches the model rather than relying on prompt-level instructions to withhold it.

Name: System Prompt Leak Exposes Internal Tool Names and Permissions to End User
Synopsis: A user query caused the agent's system prompt to leak, revealing the names and permission scopes of internal tools it has access to.
Solution: Keep tool names/permission details out of any system-prompt content that could be echoed, and apply output filtering to catch attempts to enumerate an agent's own capabilities.

Name: Training Data Poisoning via Crowdsourced Feedback Loop in Recommendation Engine
Synopsis: An attacker submitted crafted feedback that performs training data poisoning against the recommendation engine's continuous fine-tuning loop, biasing future rankings.
Solution: Restrict who can contribute to a continuously-retrained feedback loop and run anomaly detection over incoming feedback before it influences the next training pass.

Name: Backdoored Model Activates Malicious Behavior on Rare Trigger Phrase
Synopsis: The deployed model behaves as a backdoored model, producing an attacker-chosen output whenever a specific rare trigger phrase appears in its input.
Solution: Validate model behavior against adversarial test cases (not just standard accuracy benchmarks) before every deployment, specifically probing for trigger-conditioned behavior.

Name: Data Poisoning of Fraud Detection Training Set Suppresses Specific Transaction Pattern
Synopsis: An insider contributed mislabeled records that constitute data poisoning of the fraud detection model's training set, causing it to systematically miss one attacker-known transaction pattern.
Solution: Restrict and audit who can contribute labeled training data, and monitor for statistically anomalous label patterns before a retrain is accepted into production.

Name: Model Poisoning via Unvetted Third-Party Fine-Tuning Dataset
Synopsis: The fine-tuning pipeline ingested an unvetted third-party dataset without validation, a model poisoning risk since the dataset's provenance and content were never independently verified.
Solution: Vet every training/fine-tuning data source's provenance before use, and run anomaly detection over the dataset prior to any fine-tuning run.

Name: Training Data Poisoning Through Unmoderated User-Submitted Content Corpus
Synopsis: Unmoderated user-submitted content was included in the training corpus without filtering, a training data poisoning exposure since any contributor could influence future model behavior.
Solution: Moderate and filter user-submitted content before it enters any training corpus, and restrict contribution volume per contributor to limit any single actor's influence.

Name: Backdoored Model Checkpoint Downloaded from Unverified Public Repository
Synopsis: The model checkpoint currently in production was sourced from an unverified public repository and was never checked for signs of being a backdoored model.
Solution: Source model checkpoints only from verified, signed repositories, and validate any externally-sourced model against known-good benchmarks before deployment.

Name: Data Poisoning Risk from Lack of Anomaly Detection on Fine-Tuning Pipeline
Synopsis: The fine-tuning pipeline has no anomaly detection over incoming training data, leaving it exposed to data poisoning from a compromised or malicious contributor.
Solution: Add anomaly detection over the fine-tuning pipeline's input data as a standing control, not just a one-time check.

Name: Model Poisoning via Label-Flipping Attack on Content Moderation Training Set
Synopsis: A label-flipping attack against the content moderation model's training set is a form of model poisoning, degrading its ability to catch a specific category of disallowed content.
Solution: Audit label sources and run periodic label-consistency checks against the moderation training set to catch a flipping attack before it affects production behavior.

Name: Training Data Poisoning Through Compromised Data-Labeling Vendor Pipeline
Synopsis: The third-party data-labeling vendor's pipeline was compromised, introducing a training data poisoning risk into the next scheduled model refresh.
Solution: Treat a labeling vendor's pipeline as part of the ML supply chain requiring the same vetting/monitoring as any other third-party data source, and hold the next scheduled refresh pending re-verification.

Name: Backdoored Model Suspected After Anomalous Behavior on Specific Input Class
Synopsis: Anomalous, consistently-wrong behavior on one narrow input class raised suspicion that the production model is a backdoored model rather than exhibiting ordinary error.
Solution: Investigate the anomalous input class specifically for trigger-conditioned behavior, and roll back to a known-good checkpoint pending confirmation.

Name: Model Registry Loads Third-Party Checkpoint via Insecure Pickle Deserialization
Synopsis: The model registry loads third-party model checkpoints using Python's pickle format without weights_only=True - insecure pickle deserialization that would execute arbitrary code if a malicious model were substituted.
Solution: Load model checkpoints with a safe loader (e.g. weights_only=True or an equivalent format-restricted loader), never a general-purpose pickle load, for any externally-sourced artifact.

Name: Malicious Pre-Trained Model Downloaded from Unofficial Mirror Site
Synopsis: A pre-trained model was downloaded from an unofficial mirror rather than the vendor's verified source, raising the risk it is a malicious pre-trained model repackaged with a hidden backdoor.
Solution: Source pre-trained models only from verified, signed vendor repositories, and re-download from the official source rather than trusting an unofficial mirror.

Name: Unsafe Deserialization of Uploaded Model File in Self-Service ML Platform
Synopsis: The self-service ML platform accepts user-uploaded model files and loads them via unsafe deserialization, allowing arbitrary code execution if a malicious model is uploaded.
Solution: Scan uploaded model artifacts for unsafe deserialization patterns and load them only through a sandboxed, format-restricted loader, never a general-purpose deserializer.

Name: Compromised ML Library Dependency Enables Insecure Deserialization of Cached Model Metadata
Synopsis: A transitive ML library dependency was compromised in a supply-chain attack, introducing a code path that performs insecure deserialization of cached model metadata - an AI supply-chain risk if paired with a malicious pre-trained model swap.
Solution: Maintain an SBOM covering ML libraries specifically, pin and vet third-party ML library versions the same as any other dependency, and patch immediately once a compromised transitive dependency is identified.

Name: Insecure Pickle Deserialization When Loading Cached Inference Artifacts
Synopsis: Cached inference artifacts are loaded via insecure pickle deserialization without integrity verification, allowing a tampered cache entry to execute arbitrary code.
Solution: Verify cache integrity (e.g. a signature or checksum) before loading, and switch cached-artifact loading to a safe, format-restricted deserializer.

Name: No SBOM Coverage for ML Model Artifacts Used in Production Inference Service
Synopsis: The production inference service has no SBOM entry for its model artifacts, an AI supply-chain gap since a malicious pre-trained model swap would go undetected.
Solution: Extend SBOM coverage to model artifacts alongside traditional application dependencies, so any unexpected model swap is detectable.

Name: Unsigned Model Artifact Accepted Without Provenance Verification
Synopsis: The deployment pipeline accepts an unsigned model artifact with no provenance verification, unable to distinguish a legitimate release from a malicious pre-trained model.
Solution: Require signed model artifacts with verified provenance before any production deployment step will accept them.

Name: Insecure Deserialization of Model Config Enables Arbitrary Attribute Injection
Synopsis: The model-loading step performs insecure deserialization of a YAML config bundled with the model, allowing arbitrary attribute injection if the bundle is tampered with.
Solution: Load model configuration through a schema-validated, safe parser rather than an insecure deserializer that allows arbitrary object construction.

Name: Third-Party Fine-Tuned Model Adopted Without Independent Behavioral Validation
Synopsis: A third-party fine-tuned model was adopted into production without independent behavioral validation, an AI supply-chain risk if it is in fact a malicious pre-trained model with planted behavior.
Solution: Independently validate any third-party fine-tuned model against known-good benchmarks and adversarial test cases before adopting it into production.

Name: Vulnerable Version of ML Serialization Library Enables Insecure Deserialization
Synopsis: The deployed ML serialization library version has a known insecure deserialization weakness, and the pipeline has not been updated to the patched release.
Solution: Update the ML serialization library to the patched release and pin the version going forward, treating it the same as any other vulnerable dependency.

Name: LLM Output Rendered as Unescaped HTML in Chat Widget
Synopsis: The chat widget renders LLM output directly into the page as unescaped HTML, allowing a crafted response to execute injected script in the user's browser.
Solution: Escape LLM output before rendering as HTML, exactly like this project's own escapeHtml() pattern applied to any other untrusted string.

Name: Model Output Passed to eval() to Execute Generated Automation Script
Synopsis: The automation agent passes model output directly to eval() to run a generated script, executing whatever code the model (or an attacker manipulating it) produces.
Solution: Never eval()/exec() model output; parse and execute only a constrained, pre-approved set of operations instead of arbitrary generated code.

Name: LLM Output Concatenated Unsanitized into SQL Query in Reporting Tool
Synopsis: The reporting tool builds a database query by concatenating LLM output directly into an unsanitized SQL string, allowing a crafted response to alter the query's meaning.
Solution: Parameterize any downstream query built from model output rather than string-concatenating it, the same as any other untrusted input source.

Name: Model Output Used in eval() Context to Build Dynamic Configuration
Synopsis: The deployment tool takes model output and runs it through eval() to build a configuration object, giving the model's output the ability to execute arbitrary code.
Solution: Replace eval()-based configuration construction with a schema-validated parser that accepts only well-formed configuration data, never executable code.

Name: LLM Output Rendered Unescaped in Markdown Preview Pane
Synopsis: The documentation assistant's LLM output is rendered unescaped in the markdown preview pane, allowing embedded script-like markup to execute.
Solution: Escape or sanitize LLM output before rendering it in any markdown/HTML preview surface.

Name: Model Output Piped to eval() Inside Notebook Auto-Completion Feature
Synopsis: The notebook's AI auto-completion feature pipes model output straight into eval() to preview a suggested cell's result, executing unreviewed generated code.
Solution: Require an explicit user-confirmation step before executing any AI-suggested code, never auto-execute a suggestion via eval().

Name: LLM Output Used Unescaped to Construct Shell Command in DevOps Bot
Synopsis: The DevOps bot builds a shell command using LLM output that is unescaped, letting a crafted response inject additional shell operators.
Solution: Never build a shell command via string concatenation from model output; use a parameterized subprocess call with a fixed, validated argument list.

Name: Model Output From Code-Generation Assistant Passed to eval() Before Review
Synopsis: The code-generation assistant's model output is passed to eval() for a live preview before any human review step, executing unvetted generated code.
Solution: Sandbox any live-preview execution of generated code and require human review before it runs against anything beyond a fully isolated sandbox.

Name: LLM Output Embedded Unsanitized into Outbound Email Template
Synopsis: The auto-reply feature embeds LLM output unsanitized into the outbound email's HTML template, allowing injected markup to reach recipients.
Solution: Sanitize LLM output before embedding it into any outbound content template, the same as any other untrusted content source.

Name: Model Output Routed to eval() for Dynamic Report Formatting Logic
Synopsis: The reporting pipeline routes model output to eval() to determine dynamic formatting logic, giving generated text the ability to execute code at render time.
Solution: Replace eval()-based formatting logic with a fixed, declarative formatting spec the model can only select from, never author executable code for.

Name: LLM Agent Granted Excessive Agency to Approve Financial Transactions Autonomously
Synopsis: The finance-automation agent was granted excessive agency, able to approve and execute payment transactions with no human checkpoint in the loop.
Solution: Require human-in-the-loop confirmation for any consequential financial action, regardless of how confident the agent's own reasoning appears.

Name: Autonomous Ops Agent Given Unrestricted Tool Access to Production Shell
Synopsis: The autonomous ops agent was configured with unrestricted tool access to a production shell, letting a single manipulated conversation cascade into real infrastructure changes.
Solution: Apply least-privilege scoping to every tool an agent can call, and never grant unrestricted shell access to an autonomous agent operating against production.

Name: Customer Support Agent Can Issue Refunds With No Human Approval Step
Synopsis: The support agent has no human checkpoint before issuing a refund, an excessive agency risk since a manipulated conversation could trigger unauthorized payouts.
Solution: Require a human approval step for any refund above a low, pre-approved threshold, and log every agent-initiated refund for audit.

Name: Autonomous Agent Deletes Files with Unrestricted Tool Access and No Confirmation
Synopsis: The file-management agent has unrestricted tool access to delete files with no human confirmation step, letting a single erroneous instruction cause irreversible data loss.
Solution: Require explicit human confirmation before any destructive file operation, and scope the agent's delete permissions to only what its task genuinely requires.

Name: Agent Orchestrator Chains Tool Calls With No Human Checkpoint Between Steps
Synopsis: The agent orchestrator chains multiple tool calls with no human checkpoint between steps, a form of excessive agency that lets one bad decision cascade unchecked.
Solution: Insert a human or policy checkpoint between chained tool calls for any sequence with real-world side effects, rather than allowing an uninterrupted autonomous chain.

Name: Email-Sending Agent Has Unrestricted Tool Access to Company-Wide Distribution Lists
Synopsis: The email agent has unrestricted tool access to company-wide distribution lists with no human review before sending, an excessive agency exposure for mass-communication mistakes.
Solution: Require human review before any agent-initiated send to a broad distribution list, and scope the agent's send permissions to smaller, task-specific lists by default.

Name: DevOps Agent Can Modify Production Infrastructure With No Human Approval Gate
Synopsis: The DevOps agent can modify production infrastructure directly, an excessive agency configuration since there is no human approval gate before a change is applied.
Solution: Require a human approval gate (e.g. a reviewable, generated change plan) before any agent-proposed production infrastructure change is applied.

Name: Autonomous Trading Agent Executes Trades With No Human Review of Rationale
Synopsis: The trading agent executes trades autonomously with no human review of its rationale beforehand, an excessive agency risk given the direct financial impact of a wrong decision.
Solution: Require human review of the agent's stated rationale before executing any trade above a pre-approved size, and log every autonomous decision for audit.

Name: HR Agent Granted Unrestricted Tool Access to Modify Employee Compensation Records
Synopsis: The HR assistant agent was granted unrestricted tool access to modify compensation records directly, with no human approval required for the change to take effect.
Solution: Require a human approval step for any agent-proposed compensation change, and scope the agent's tool access to read-only for sensitive HR records by default.

Name: Agent-to-Shell Bridge Allows Arbitrary Command Execution With No Human in the Loop
Synopsis: The agent-to-shell bridge allows arbitrary command execution with no human in the loop, an excessive agency design that turns any single successful manipulation of the agent into direct system access.
Solution: Replace the arbitrary-command bridge with a constrained, allowlisted set of specific operations, and require human confirmation for anything outside routine read-only checks.

Name: Unbounded Context Window Accepts Arbitrarily Large Uploaded Document
Synopsis: The summarization endpoint accepts an unbounded context input from an uploaded document with no size cap, letting a single request drive excessive inference cost.
Solution: Enforce an input-length limit on uploaded documents before they're passed to the model, sized to genuine business need.

Name: Token Flood Attack Drives Excessive Inference Cost on Public Chat Endpoint
Synopsis: A scripted token flood attack against the public chat endpoint repeatedly submits maximum-length prompts, driving up inference cost with no per-user rate limit.
Solution: Apply per-user rate limiting and cost quotas to the public chat endpoint, independent of any single request's own length limit.

Name: Model Denial of Service via Recursive Self-Prompting Agent Loop
Synopsis: An uncontrolled agent loop causes the model to repeatedly re-prompt itself, a model denial of service condition that consumes resources with no forward progress.
Solution: Enforce a hard iteration cap on any agent or tool-calling loop, and detect/terminate a loop that isn't making measurable progress toward its goal.

Name: Unbounded Consumption from Missing Per-User Rate Limit on Inference API
Synopsis: The inference API has no per-user rate limit, an unbounded consumption exposure that lets a single caller monopolize available capacity.
Solution: Add a per-user or per-API-key rate limit to the inference API as a baseline control, regardless of any other cost-management measure.

Name: Token Flood via Adversarially Crafted Repetitive Prompt Pattern
Synopsis: An adversarially crafted, highly repetitive prompt pattern constitutes a token flood, consuming disproportionate compute relative to its actual informational content.
Solution: Detect and rate-limit repetitive/low-information-density prompt patterns as a defense-in-depth cost control.

Name: Model DoS Condition from Uncontrolled Retry Loop on Failed Tool Call
Synopsis: A tool-calling agent enters an uncontrolled retry loop on a failed call, a model denial of service condition since retries are unbounded and unthrottled.
Solution: Cap retry attempts with backoff and a hard ceiling, and alert rather than retry indefinitely once the cap is reached.

Name: Unbounded Context Consumption from Unlimited Conversation History Retention
Synopsis: The chat session retains unlimited conversation history and resubmits all of it as context on every turn, an unbounded consumption pattern that scales cost with session length alone.
Solution: Cap retained conversation history (e.g. a rolling window or summarized older turns) instead of resubmitting an ever-growing transcript on every request.

Name: Token Flood Exploits Lack of Input-Length Validation on Batch Summarization Job
Synopsis: The batch summarization job has no input-length validation, letting a token flood of oversized documents drive excessive cost in a single scheduled run.
Solution: Validate and cap input length per document in the batch job, rejecting or splitting oversized documents rather than processing them unbounded.

Name: Model Denial of Service via Crafted Prompt Triggering Maximum-Length Generation
Synopsis: A crafted prompt reliably triggers maximum-length generation on every call, a model denial of service pattern that maximizes cost per request with minimal attacker effort.
Solution: Set a reasonable output-length cap tuned to genuine use cases, and monitor for prompts that consistently hit the maximum.

Name: Unbounded Consumption from Missing Iteration Cap on Autonomous Research Agent
Synopsis: The autonomous research agent has no iteration cap on its own tool-calling loop, an unbounded consumption risk that can run indefinitely on an unproductive research path.
Solution: Add a hard iteration/time cap to the research agent's loop, mirroring this project's own --max-budget-usd spend-cap pattern applied to a different cost surface.

Name: Model Extraction Attack via Systematic Query Sweep Against Public Inference API
Synopsis: A systematic, high-volume query sweep against the public inference API is consistent with a model extraction attack aimed at reconstructing the underlying model's decision boundary.
Solution: Rate-limit and monitor API query patterns for extraction-shaped behavior, such as unusually broad, systematic input coverage from one account.

Name: Model Theft Risk from Unrestricted Bulk Export of Model Weights
Synopsis: The ML platform allows any authenticated user to bulk-export model weights directly, a model theft risk with no additional access control beyond basic authentication.
Solution: Restrict raw model-artifact export to the same access-control standard as any other high-value credential or secret, not just basic authentication.

Name: Model Stealing Attempt Detected via High-Volume API Calls from Single Account
Synopsis: An unusually high volume of API calls from a single account, spanning a systematic input sweep, is consistent with a model stealing attempt against the proprietary scoring model.
Solution: Alert on and rate-limit accounts whose query volume/pattern is consistent with a model stealing attempt.

Name: Model Extraction via Distillation From Repeated Confidence-Score Queries
Synopsis: An attacker issuing repeated queries specifically to harvest confidence scores is performing model extraction via distillation, reconstructing model behavior without access to its weights.
Solution: Consider withholding or coarsening raw confidence scores in the public API response where the extra precision isn't needed by legitimate callers.

Name: Model Theft Exposure from Unencrypted Model Artifact Storage Bucket
Synopsis: The model artifact storage bucket is unencrypted and broadly readable, a model theft exposure since the raw weights could be copied directly rather than extracted via queries.
Solution: Encrypt model artifact storage at rest and restrict read access to only the services that genuinely need it.

Name: Model Stealing Risk from Missing Rate Limits on Recommendation Engine's Public API
Synopsis: The recommendation engine's public API has no rate limiting, a model stealing risk since an attacker could systematically probe it to reconstruct its ranking logic.
Solution: Add rate limiting to the recommendation engine's public API as a baseline anti-extraction control.

Name: Model Extraction Attack Pattern Identified in API Access Logs Over 30-Day Window
Synopsis: A 30-day review of API access logs identified a query pattern consistent with a model extraction attack: broad, systematic input coverage from a small number of accounts.
Solution: Investigate and rate-limit the identified accounts, and add ongoing monitoring for the same query-pattern signature going forward.

Name: Model Theft via Insufficient Access Control on Internal Model-Serving Endpoint
Synopsis: An internal model-serving endpoint intended for one team is reachable more broadly than intended, a model theft exposure since it returns full output the raw model would produce.
Solution: Restrict the internal model-serving endpoint's access control to the specific team/service it was intended for.

Name: Model Stealing Countermeasure Missing: No Watermarking on Generated Outputs
Synopsis: The deployed model has no output watermarking, leaving no way to detect model stealing via a competitor training on scraped outputs.
Solution: Evaluate output watermarking where feasible for the model's output type, as a detective (not preventive) control against distillation-based model stealing.

Name: Model Extraction Risk from Verbose Error Messages Revealing Internal Model Structure
Synopsis: Verbose error messages returned by the inference API reveal internal model structure details, aiding a model extraction attempt by narrowing the attacker's search space.
Solution: Return generic error messages to API callers and log verbose details only server-side.

Name: Model Hallucinates Fabricated Legal Citation Presented as Fact to End User
Synopsis: The legal-research assistant hallucinates a fabricated case citation and presents it as fact, with no confidence indicator to signal the claim is unverified.
Solution: Require citation verification against a real source before presenting any legal reference as fact, and surface confidence/uncertainty in the response.

Name: Overreliance on Model Output Without Human Review in Automated Decision Pipeline
Synopsis: The automated decision pipeline exhibits overreliance on model output, acting on generated conclusions with no human review step before a consequential action is taken.
Solution: Add a human review step before any consequential automated action, and never let unreviewed model output alone trigger it.

Name: Model Hallucinates Non-Existent API Endpoint in Generated Integration Code
Synopsis: The coding assistant hallucinates a plausible-sounding but non-existent API endpoint, which a developer could ship without independently verifying it exists.
Solution: Verify any AI-suggested API reference against real documentation before shipping generated integration code.

Name: Misinformation Risk: Model Presents Uncertain Medical Guidance as Definitive
Synopsis: The health-information model presents an uncertain claim as definitive guidance, a misinformation risk in a model deployed without a clear uncertainty-disclosure mechanism.
Solution: Surface confidence/uncertainty explicitly wherever the underlying model exposes it, and never present an uncertain health claim as definitive.

Name: Model Hallucinates Financial Figures in Automated Quarterly Summary Draft
Synopsis: The reporting assistant hallucinates a plausible-looking financial figure in its automated summary draft, which was nearly published without cross-checking against the source data.
Solution: Cross-check any generated figure against the underlying source data before publication, and keep a human reviewer in the loop for financial reporting content.

Name: Overreliance on Model-Generated Risk Score Without Independent Verification
Synopsis: The underwriting workflow exhibits overreliance on a model-generated risk score, treating it as authoritative with no independent verification step before a decision is finalized.
Solution: Add an independent verification step before finalizing a decision based on a model-generated score, rather than treating it as authoritative on its own.

Name: Model Hallucinates Source Attribution for a Claim It Cannot Actually Support
Synopsis: The research assistant hallucinates a specific source attribution for a claim, citing a document that does not actually contain the claimed information.
Solution: Verify cited sources actually support the attributed claim before surfacing the citation, rather than trusting the model's own attribution.

Name: Misinformation Concern: Model Confidently Answers Outside Its Verified Knowledge Scope
Synopsis: The support model answers confidently on topics outside its verified knowledge scope, a misinformation risk since nothing in its response signals the lower reliability.
Solution: Constrain the model's confident-answer scope to its verified knowledge domain, and surface an explicit lower-confidence signal outside that scope.

Name: Model Hallucinates Plausible but Incorrect Regulatory Requirement in Compliance Assistant
Synopsis: The compliance assistant hallucinates a plausible-sounding but incorrect regulatory requirement, which was surfaced to an analyst as though it were an established rule.
Solution: Require verification against the actual regulatory text before presenting any compliance requirement as established, and keep a human reviewer in the loop.

Name: Overreliance on Chatbot Guidance Led to Incorrect Customer-Facing Policy Statement
Synopsis: Overreliance on the chatbot's generated guidance, without a human review step, led to an incorrect policy statement being sent directly to a customer.
Solution: Add a human review step before any AI-generated policy statement reaches a customer, rather than sending unreviewed guidance directly.

Name: File-System Plugin Accepts Unvalidated Path Input From LLM Agent
Synopsis: The file-system plugin invoked by the LLM agent accepts an unvalidated path argument directly from model output, allowing path traversal outside the intended directory.
Solution: Validate and constrain the plugin's path argument at the tool boundary itself, rejecting any path outside an explicit allowlisted directory.

Name: Payment Plugin Processes Unvalidated Amount Field Supplied by Agent
Synopsis: The payment-processing plugin accepts an unvalidated amount field passed directly from the agent's tool call, with no server-side bounds checking before executing the charge.
Solution: Validate the amount field against server-side bounds and business rules at the plugin boundary, independent of whatever the agent supplies.

Name: Tool-Calling Interface Executes Unvalidated Shell Argument From Model Output
Synopsis: The tool-calling interface passes an unvalidated argument straight from model output into a shell command, extending an attacker's reach from the conversation into the underlying system.
Solution: Never build a shell command from unvalidated model output; use a parameterized call with a fixed, validated argument list at the tool boundary.

Name: Internal API Plugin Accepts Unvalidated Request Body Constructed by Agent
Synopsis: The internal API plugin accepts an unvalidated request body constructed entirely by the agent, trusting the model to always produce well-formed, safe arguments.
Solution: Validate the plugin's request body against a strict schema at the tool boundary, never trusting the model to only ever pass well-formed arguments.

Name: Database Query Plugin Passes Unvalidated Filter Clause From LLM Agent Tool Call
Synopsis: The database-query plugin passes an unvalidated filter clause directly from the LLM agent's tool call into the query builder, allowing an unintended broad or malicious filter.
Solution: Constrain the plugin to a fixed set of parameterized filter options rather than accepting a free-form, unvalidated filter clause from the agent.

Name: Tool-Calling Framework Allows Unvalidated Recipient Field in Email-Sending Tool
Synopsis: The tool-calling framework's email tool accepts an unvalidated recipient field from the agent, allowing a manipulated conversation to redirect messages to an unintended address.
Solution: Validate the recipient field against an allowlist or existing-contact check at the tool boundary, independent of what the agent supplies.

Name: Webhook-Triggering Plugin Accepts Unvalidated URL From Agent Without Allowlist
Synopsis: The webhook plugin accepts an unvalidated destination URL supplied by the agent with no allowlist, letting a manipulated agent trigger a request to an arbitrary endpoint.
Solution: Restrict the webhook plugin to a pre-approved destination allowlist, rejecting any URL supplied by the agent that isn't on it.

Name: Calendar-Modifying Plugin Trusts Unvalidated Date Range Supplied by LLM Agent
Synopsis: The calendar plugin trusts an unvalidated date range supplied directly by the LLM agent, with no bounds check before bulk-modifying events in that range.
Solution: Bounds-check the date range at the plugin boundary and require confirmation before any bulk-modification action.

Name: Code-Execution Plugin Accepts Unvalidated Script Body From Tool-Calling Agent
Synopsis: The code-execution plugin accepts an unvalidated script body passed directly from the tool-calling agent, running it with no sandboxing or review step.
Solution: Sandbox any agent-invoked code execution and require human review before running a generated script outside a fully isolated environment.

Name: Ticketing-System Plugin Accepts Unvalidated Priority Escalation Field From Agent
Synopsis: The ticketing-system plugin accepts an unvalidated priority-escalation field from the agent's tool call, letting a manipulated conversation force incident escalation.
Solution: Validate the escalation field against role-based limits at the plugin boundary, rather than trusting whatever priority the agent's tool call requests.
